en: Sutta Nipāta 3.7 Selasutta Thus have I heard—

On one occasion, while the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Aṅguttarāpas with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus—numbering twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus—he arrived at a market town of the Aṅguttarāpas named Āpaṇa.
The matted-hair ascetic Keṇiya heard:

"The recluse Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, is indeed wandering on tour among the Aṅguttarāpas with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus—numbering twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus—and has arrived at Āpaṇa."
Furthermore, this excellent report of the venerable Gotama has spread abroad:

"Indeed, that Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with clear knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having realized this world—with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—by his own direct higher knowledge, he makes it known.
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
It is indeed good to see such Arahants.
Then Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side.
As Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic was sitting there, the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then, having been instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One’s discourse on the Dhamma, Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic said this to the Blessed One:
“May the venerable Gotama accept tomorrow’s meal from me, together with the community of bhikkhus.
When this was said, the Blessed One said to Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic:
“The community of bhikkhus is large, Keṇiya—there are twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus—and you have great confidence in the brahmins.”
A second time, Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic said this to the Blessed One:
“Even though, Master Gotama, there is a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus— numbering twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus— and I am well-disposed toward the brahmins,
may Master Gotama together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus accept my meal for tomorrow.”
A second time, the Blessed One said this to Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic:
“Keṇiya, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is large—there are twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus—and you have great faith in the brahmins.
A third time, Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic said this to the Blessed One:
“Even though, Master Gotama, there is a great community of monks consisting of twelve hundred and fifty monks, and I myself am devoted to the brahmins,
may the Blessed One Gotama, together with the community of monks, accept my meal for tomorrow.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.

Then Keṇiya the coiled-hair ascetic, having understood the Blessed One’s acceptance, rose from his seat and went to his own hermitage. Having arrived, he addressed his friends, companions, kinsmen, and relatives:
"Listen, sirs, my friends, companions, kinsmen, and relatives!
I have invited the ascetic Gotama, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, for tomorrow's meal."
“...so that you may perform services for my body.
“Very well, sir,” Keṇiya’s friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations replied to Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic.
Some of them dug out hearths; some split wood; and some prepared the vessels.
Some were washing [the floor], some were setting out water-jars, and some were preparing seats.
Meanwhile, the matted-hair ascetic Keṇiya himself was preparing the circular pavilion.
Now at that time, the brahmin Sela was staying in the marketplace; he was a master of the three Vedas, including the Nighaṇḍu and the Keṭubha.
He was a master of the Vedas, including the Itihāsas as the fifth, a lexicographer, a grammarian, and one well-versed in Lokāyata philosophy and the marks of a Great Man;
he taught the mantras to three hundred young brahmins.
At that time, Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic was deeply devoted to the brahmin Seḷa.
Then the brahmin Sela, accompanied by three hundred young brahmins, while walking and wandering for exercise, approached the hermitage of Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic.
There he saw some people digging hearths in Keṇiya’s hermitage... [and so on] ...some preparing seats, while Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic himself was preparing the circular pavilion.
Having seen this, he said to Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic:
“Is there perhaps to be a wedding for Master Keṇiya, or a marriage, or has a great sacrifice been prepared, or has King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha been invited together with his army for tomorrow?
“There will be no wedding for me, sir Sela, nor a marriage; nor has King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha been invited together with his army for tomorrow.
Rather, a great sacrifice has been prepared for me.”

"There is the ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from a Sakyan clan; while wandering on tour among the Aṅguttarāpas with a great saṅgha of bhikkhus, numbering twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus, he has arrived at Āpaṇa.
That venerable Gotama is ... [as before] ...
a Buddha, a Blessed One."
“Thus I have been invited by him, together with the community of monks, for tomorrow’s meal.
“‘Buddha,’ sir Keṇiya, do you say?
“‘Buddha,’ sir Sela, I say.”
“‘Buddha,’ Master Keṇiya, do you say?
“‘Buddha,’ Master Sela, I say.
Then this thought occurred to the brahmin Sela:
“Even this sound, ‘Buddha,’ is rare in the world.
Now, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man have come down to us in our mantras; for a Great Man endowed with these, there are only two possible destinies and no other.

If he dwells at home, he becomes a king, a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a king of Dharma, conqueror of the four quarters, who has established stability in the land and is possessed of the seven treasures.”
For him there are these seven treasures, namely:
the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh.
Moreover, he has more than a thousand sons who are brave, heroic in form, and crushers of enemy armies.
Thus he dwells having conquered this earth, bounded by the ocean, without stick or sword, by means of the Dhamma.
But if he goes forth from the home life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha who has drawn back the veil from the world.
Now, Master Keṇiya, where is that venerable Gotama, the Arahant, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, dwelling at present?”
When this was said, Keṇiya the coiled-hair ascetic raised his right arm and said to the brahmin Sela:
“In that direction, Master Sela, where that row of dark-blue forest stands.
Then the brahmin Sela, together with three hundred young brahmin students, approached the Blessed One.
Then the brahmin Sela addressed those young men:
"Come, sirs, with little noise, placing one foot down after the other;
for those Blessed Ones are difficult to approach, solitary like lions."
"And when I am conversing with the ascetic Gotama, sirs, do not interrupt my speech from time to time;
may you wait until the conclusion of my discourse.
Then the brahmin Sela approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasanter conversation with him, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the brahmin Sela examined the Blessed One’s body for the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
The brahmin Sela saw the thirty-two marks of a Great Man on the Blessed One’s body, with the exception of two.
He was doubtful, perplexed, undecided, and lacked confidence regarding two of the marks of a Great Man:
the male organ being sheathed and the possession of a long tongue.
Then this occurred to the Blessed One:
“This brahmin Sela has indeed seen in me most of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, with the exception of two.
Regarding two of these marks of a Great Man, he is doubtful, perplexed, undecided, and lacks confidence:
namely, the sheathed genitals and the large tongue.”
Then the Blessed One performed such a feat of psychic power that the brahmin Sela saw the Blessed One’s private parts withdrawn in a sheath.
Then the Blessed One, having extended his tongue, touched and rubbed both ear-holes, he touched and rubbed both nostrils, and he covered his entire forehead with his tongue.
Then it occurred to the brahmin Sela:
“The ascetic Gotama is indeed endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, complete and not incomplete.
Yet I do not know whether he is a Buddha or not.
However, I have heard this from aged and elderly brahmins, the teachers of teachers, as they were speaking:”
“Those who are Worthy Ones, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, reveal themselves when their own praise is being spoken.
What if I were to extol the ascetic Gotama in his presence with appropriate verses?
Then the brahmin Sela extolled the Blessed One in his presence with appropriate verses:
“With a perfect body, Suruci,
well-born and lovely to behold;
you are golden-hued, O Blessed One.”
You have beautiful teeth and are full of vigor;
for such are the characteristics that belong to a well-born man.
All those marks of a Great Man are upon your body;
you have clear eyes and a beautiful face.
Tall, straight, and majestic,
you shine like the sun in the midst of the community of ascetics.
The monk of auspicious appearance,
with skin like refined gold—
what use have you for the state of a recluse?
Thus, O one of supreme beauty,
you are worthy to be a king,
a wheel-turning monarch, a bull among charioteers.
A conqueror of the four quarters,
lord of the Jambusaṇḍa,
a kshatriya, a sovereign king of wealth.
Let them be your followers;
O Gotama, as a king of kings, a lord of men, exercise sovereignty.”
“I am a king, O rock,” [said] the Blessed One,
“an unsurpassed King of Dhamma.”
“I turn the wheel by means of the Dhamma,
a wheel that cannot be turned back.
“You claim to be a Perfectly Awakened One;”
(Thus spoke the brahmin Sela:
"The peerless King of Dhamma:
'By means of Dhamma I turn the wheel.'"
"Thus you speak, Gotama.
Who indeed is your general,
the disciple who follows in the Teacher's footsteps?"
"Who follows you,
who has set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma?
"The wheel set in motion by me..."
(The Blessed One said:
"Sāriputta turns the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma in accordance with it."
He is born after the Tathāgata.
That which is to be directly known has been directly known;
that which is to be developed has been developed.
What was to be abandoned has been abandoned by me;
therefore, O Brahmin, I am a Buddha.
Let you dispel your doubt regarding me.
Have faith, O Brahmin;
for the frequent sight of the Fully Enlightened Ones is difficult to obtain.
O Brahmin, I am that perfectly awakened one whose manifestation is indeed rare in this world and does not occur frequently.
The unsurpassed surgeon,
become like Brahmā, incomparable,
the crusher of Māra’s army;
"Having brought all friends under my control,
I rejoice, free from fear from any quarter.
Listen to this, sirs!"
As the one with vision speaks,
the great hero, the surgeon,
roars like a lion in the forest.
Who, having seen him who has become Brahmā, the incomparable,
the crusher of Māra’s army,
would not be filled with faith?
Even one of dark birth—
let him who wishes follow me,
or let him who does not wish go.
"Here I shall go forth into homelessness in the presence of the one of supreme wisdom.
"If this is indeed your wish, sir,"
“In the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One,
we too shall go forth into homelessness in the presence of him of supreme wisdom.”
These three hundred brahmins,
with palms joined in reverence, entreat you:
"We shall lead the holy life."
“The Blessed One is in your presence.
“The holy life is well-expounded,” said the Blessed One (to Sela).
Visible here and now, not subject to time;
wherein renunciation is not in vain for one who trains with diligence.
The brahmin Sela, together with his retinue, received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One and received full ordination.
Then, at the end of that night, Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic had various kinds of fine food, both hard and soft, prepared in his own hermitage and had the time announced to the Blessed One, saying:
"It is time, Master Gotama; the meal is ready."

Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, approached the hermitage of Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat together with the community of monks.
Then Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic, with his own hands, personally satisfied and served the community of monks headed by the Buddha with excellent hard and soft foods.
When the Blessed One had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
As Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic sat to one side, the Blessed One expressed his appreciation with these verses:
“Sacrifices have the fire-oblation as their chief;
the Sāvitti is the chief of Vedic meters;”
The king is the mouth of men;
the ocean is the mouth of rivers;
the moon is the mouth of the constellations.
The sun is the chief of all that gives heat;
the Saṅgha is indeed the chief of those who sacrifice, for those desiring merit.
Then the Blessed One, having expressed his appreciation to the matted-hair ascetic Keṇiya with these verses, rose from his seat and departed. Then the Venerable Sela,
dwelling alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute together with his followers, before long— [as it is said]—
the Venerable Sela and his followers became arahants.

Then the Venerable Sela, together with his retinue, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he arranged his robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“O Seer, it is now the eighth day since we came to you for refuge.”
In seven nights, O Blessed One, we have been tamed in your teaching.
You are the Buddha; you are the Teacher.
You are the Sage who has overcome Māra;
having severed the underlying tendencies,
you have crossed over and are now able to ferry this generation across.
You have transcended all acquisitions;
your taints are shattered.
You are a lion, free from clinging.
These three hundred bhikkhus, having abandoned fear and terror,
stand with their hands joined in reverential salutation.
“Stretch out your feet, O Hero;
let the Nāgas pay homage to the Teacher.
The seventh discourse, the Sela Sutta, is concluded.
